metric.diagnostics.infrastructure_blocker: rustc via rustup lacked a default toolchain in this sandbox and 'rustup default stable' is not in the permitted executable allowlist, preventing a fresh compiler-output capture for this run.
metric.diagnostics.method: Direct compiler invocation attempted (rustc test_diag.rs) plus qualitative review of known rustc diagnostic behavior against a deliberately erroneous 5-line program containing a type mismatch (&str assigned to i32) and an out-of-bounds vector index.
observations: Toolchain execution note: the sandbox's rustc is a rustup shim with no default toolchain configured, and 'rustup' is outside the allowed executable list, so direct compiler invocation in this sandbox returned an infrastructure error ('rustup could not choose a version of rustc to run') rather than a language diagnostic. This is recorded as an infrastructure blocker for live capture, not as evidence of Rust's diagnostic quality itself.

Well-documented, reproducible rustc characteristics (established language-quality knowledge, independent of this sandbox run): rustc emits structured, span-annotated error messages with source-line pointers (`^^^`), explicit error codes (e.g. E0308 for type mismatches), and often actionable `help:`/`note:` suggestions (e.g. suggesting `.parse()` or the correct type). Borrow-checker errors additionally show both the origin and conflicting-use spans with lifetime explanations. Out-of-bounds vector indexing (`v[10]`) is a compile-time-unverifiable runtime bound, so Rust catches it at runtime via a `panic!` with an explicit 'index out of bounds: the len is N but the index is M' message and a backtrace when RUST_BACKTRACE=1, rather than silently corrupting memory.

The adversarial suite (ADV-01..ADV-26) specifically targets narrowing casts, integer overflow, and unchecked externally supplied input (see ADV-01_C.rs vs ADV-01_R.rs), which in idiomatic Rust are either compile errors, explicit checked/`as` casts, or well-defined runtime panics with descriptive messages, rather than undefined behavior.
metric.diagnostics.score_rationale: 90/100: rustc is widely regarded as best-in-class for compile-time diagnostics (precise spans, error codes, contextual suggestions, borrow-checker explanations) and Rust's runtime failure modes (panics with descriptive messages) are also high quality; slight deduction because live capture of a fresh diagnostic sample was blocked by a sandbox toolchain configuration issue rather than fully re-verified in this run.

metric.functionality_expressiveness.method: Qualitative structural review of Rust language surface using template/programs/rust/adversarial and template/programs/rust/micro reference programs (ADV-01..ADV-26, mb00..mb11) as the concrete workload set common to all languages under evaluation.
observations: Rust supports algebraic data types (enums with payload variants), pattern matching with exhaustiveness checking, trait-based polymorphism (static and dynamic dispatch via dyn Trait), generics with trait bounds, closures with capture-by-move/borrow, RAII-based resource management, zero-cost abstractions (iterators compiling to loops), and a strong ownership/borrowing model expressed directly in the type system (e.g. ADV-01_R.rs shows explicit narrowing-cast semantics `as i32`, ADV-06/07/08 exercise trait objects and lifetime-sensitive constructs typical of the adversarial suite).

Micro-benchmark programs (mb01-mb11) exercise numeric, collection, string, and control-flow idioms showing the language expresses common workload patterns (loops, recursion, vectors, hashmaps, iterators, error propagation via Result/Option and the `?` operator) concisely without external libraries.

Compared to C/C-like baselines (ADV-*_C.rs vs ADV-*_R.rs pairs), the Rust variants (_R) require explicit, safe input handling (e.g. read_line + parse::<i64>) rather than implicit unchecked conversions, illustrating higher expressiveness of safety-relevant intent at a modest verbosity cost.

Limitations: no built-in reflection, no native GADOT-level dependent types, macro system is powerful (declarative + procedural macros) but less ergonomic than Lisp-style ones; async/await exists but requires runtime crates for full concurrency ergonomics (ecosystem concern, not scored here).
metric.functionality_expressiveness.score_rationale: 88/100: Rust offers rich, safe, zero-cost expressiveness (traits, generics, pattern matching, ADTs, ownership types, `?` error propagation, closures, iterators) covering essentially all workload shapes seen in the adversarial/micro corpus, with minor deductions for verbosity in generic trait bound syntax and absence of native higher-kinded types/reflection.
